```{r, include = FALSE}
have_survey <- requireNamespace("survey", quietly = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  eval = have_survey
)

build_rich_tables <- identical(Sys.getenv("IN_PKGDOWN"), "true")
have_me <- have_survey && requireNamespace("marginaleffects", quietly = TRUE)
have_gt <- have_survey && requireNamespace("gt", quietly = TRUE)
source("_pkgdown-helpers.R")
```

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(spicy)
library(survey) # svydesign(), svyglm(), svyolr(), svycoxph()
```

This article covers regression on data from a complex survey: models
fitted with the survey package (Lumley, 2004) on a declared design,
`svyglm()`, `svyolr()` and `svycoxph()`. The descriptive side of the
same designs is in [*Summary tables from a survey
design*](survey-tables.html). The companion article
[*Publication-ready regression tables*](table-regression.html) covers
the shared mechanics (output engines, labels, `tidy()`), and the
class-by-class map is [*Supported
models*](table-regression-supported-models.html).

## Why a design, and what it changes

A survey sample is rarely a simple random sample. Units are drawn with
unequal probabilities, within strata, and often in clusters: schools
within districts, households within census tracts. Design-based
inference takes that selection mechanism as the source of randomness.
In Binder's words, "the probabilities used to select the sample are
then used as the basis for statistical inference, and such inference
refers back to the finite population from which the random sample was
selected" (Binder, 2008, p. 191).

For a regression table, this has consequences in three places.

The coefficients solve weighted estimating equations. The estimator is
a pseudo-maximum likelihood estimator (Binder, 1992, p. 141): it has
the form of a likelihood equation, but the sample has no likelihood
under the design. Everything that needs one is therefore missing, the
likelihood-ratio test and the usual AIC first.

The variance comes from the design. Strata, clusters and a finite
population correction all enter it, by linearization or by replicate
weights. The weights alone do not determine it.

The reference distribution of the tests comes from the design too. Its
degrees of freedom are counted on the primary sampling units, not on
the rows.

Whether a regression should be weighted at all is a modelling question
that no table settles. When the sampling is informative, model-based
estimates "can be severely biased" (Binder, 2008, p. 193), and "the
appropriateness of the weighted regression estimate depends on which
model is chosen" (DuMouchel & Duncan, 1983, p. 535). This article starts
after that decision: the analysis is design-based, and the question is
how to report it.

## The designs used here

The examples use the data that ship with survey. The `api` data hold
the Academic Performance Index of Californian schools, with several
samples of the same population: `apiclus1` is a cluster sample of 15
school districts, `apistrat` a sample stratified by school type. The
`nhanes` data are an extract of NHANES 2009-2010 on high cholesterol,
with the strata, the primary sampling units and the examination
weights of the survey.

```{r designs}
data(api)
data(nhanes)

dclus1 <- svydesign(id = ~dnum, weights = ~pw, data = apiclus1, fpc = ~fpc)

nhanes$race <- factor(
  nhanes$race,
  levels = 1:4,
  labels = c("Hispanic", "White", "Black", "Other")
)
nhanes$sex <- factor(
  nhanes$RIAGENDR,
  levels = 1:2,
  labels = c("Male", "Female")
)
dnh <- svydesign(
  id = ~SDMVPSU, strata = ~SDMVSTRA, weights = ~WTMEC2YR,
  nest = TRUE, data = nhanes
)
dnh
```

## A first table

A linear model of the school's score in 2000 on three characteristics
of its pupils: the percentage of English language learners (`ell`), the
percentage eligible for subsidized meals (`meals`), and the percentage
in their first year at the school (`mobility`).

```{r first-table}
gl <- svyglm(api00 ~ ell + meals + mobility, design = dclus1)
table_regression(gl)
```

The coefficients, the standard errors and the p-values are those of
`summary(gl)`: `table_regression()` reads a design-based fit and
computes none of its inference. What it adds is in the fit statistics
and the note.

* `n` is the number of schools in the sample. `Weighted n` is the sum
  of their design weights, the 6,194 schools of the population the
  estimates describe.
* The design line of the note states what was declared, here a cluster
  sample of 15 PSUs with a finite population correction, and the
  degrees of freedom the tests of the table use.
* `Std. errors: design-based (Taylor linearization)` names the
  variance estimator. Linearization "uses the linear terms of a Taylor
  series expansion to approximate the estimator by a linear function of
  the observed data" (Williams, 2008, p. 876).

On the substance, a school loses 3.1 points of API for each additional
percentage point of pupils eligible for subsidized meals, with a 95%
interval from 2.5 to 3.7 points. The two other coefficients are not
distinguishable from zero in this sample.

## Degrees of freedom come from the PSUs

The table above rests on 183 schools and tests with 11 degrees of
freedom.

```{r df}
c(rows = nrow(apiclus1), design = degf(dclus1), model = df.residual(gl))
```

The sample is a sample of 15 districts, and the schools of a district
were taken together. Clustering "results in fewer degrees of freedom in
the sense that the sample now focuses on a smaller number of sampling
units, that is, the first-stage clusters" (Lavrakas, 2008, p. 787). The
design has 15 PSUs in one stratum, hence 14 degrees of freedom, and
survey takes the residual degrees of freedom of the model by
subtraction: its help page says the rule "is correct for PSU-level
covariates but is potentially very conservative for individual-level
covariates" (`?svyglm`, survey 4.5). Three predictors leave 11.

`table_regression()` reads that number on the fit and never derives it:
the engines of survey do not share one rule, and a Cox fit ends one
degree of freedom above what the same arithmetic gives for a
`svyglm()`. `survey::regTermTest()` takes the same number as the
denominator of its F test.

The consequence is visible in every interval of the table. With 11
degrees of freedom the t quantile is 12% larger than the normal one:

```{r df-ratio}
qt(0.975, df.residual(gl)) / qnorm(0.975)
```

A large file does not protect against this. The NHANES extract has
7,846 respondents with a cholesterol measure, drawn from 31 PSUs in 15
strata: 16 degrees of freedom for the design, and each coefficient of a
model takes one of them.

## Weights are not a design

`lm()` and `glm()` accept a `weights` argument, and passing the
sampling weights there gives the right coefficients. It does not give
the right inference. The same model, both ways:

```{r weights-linear}
lw <- lm(api00 ~ ell + meals + mobility, data = apiclus1, weights = pw)
table_regression(
  list("lm(weights = pw)" = lw, "svyglm(design)" = gl),
  show_columns = c("b", "se", "p")
)
```

The two columns of coefficients are identical. The standard error of
the intercept doubles under the design, from 10.45 to 21.39, and that of
`meals` goes from 0.21 to 0.28. `lm()` treats the 183 schools as
independent draws, and reads each weight as a precision. The `R²` row
is filled for the `lm()` only: spicy reports no R² for a design-based
fit.

The error does not always run in the same direction. A logistic model
of high cholesterol on NHANES, with the weights rescaled to average 1
for `glm()`:

```{r weights-logit}
fit <- svyglm(
  HI_CHOL ~ agecat + race + sex,
  design = dnh,
  family = quasibinomial
)

nh <- subset(nhanes, !is.na(HI_CHOL))
nh$w <- nh$WTMEC2YR / mean(nh$WTMEC2YR)
naive <- glm(
  HI_CHOL ~ agecat + race + sex,
  data = nh,
  family = quasibinomial,
  weights = w
)

table_regression(
  list("glm(weights = )" = naive, "svyglm(design)" = fit),
  show_columns = c("b", "se", "p")
)
```

```{r se-ratio}
round(SE(fit) / sqrt(diag(vcov(naive))), 2)
```

The design-based standard errors range from 0.73 to 1.92 times those
of the weighted `glm()`, and the p-values move with them: `Female` from
.004 to .033, `Black` from .007 to .019, `White` from .437 to .316. The
weighted `glm()` is neither conservative nor liberal, so it cannot
serve as a bound. Its tests also refer to 7,838 residual degrees of
freedom, where the design has 9.

Both fits use `family = quasibinomial`. For `svyglm()` this is the
convention of survey: the quasi families "give the same point estimates
and standard errors" as `binomial` and avoid a warning about
non-integer numbers of successes (`?svyglm`).

## A logistic model on NHANES

```{r logit}
table_regression(fit, exponentiate = TRUE)
```

With `exponentiate = TRUE` the coefficients are odds ratios, the
standard errors are on the odds-ratio scale by the delta method, and
the intervals are the exponentiated bounds of the intervals on the
log-odds scale, which is why they are not symmetric. The note says all
three.

Age dominates. Compared with respondents of 19 or younger, the odds of
high cholesterol are about 10 times higher between 20 and 39, and 20 to
25 times higher after 40. The intervals are wide, from 4.7 to 20.5 for
the first of these odds ratios: they carry the 9 degrees of freedom of
the design. Women have higher odds than men, 1.24 times, with an
interval that starts at 1.02.

## Average marginal effects under the design

An odds ratio of 1.24 says nothing about how many more women than men
have high cholesterol. The average marginal effect answers on the
probability scale.

```{r ame, eval = have_me}
table_regression(fit, show_columns = c("b", "ame", "ame_ci", "ame_p"))
```

At the same age group and race, the probability of high cholesterol is
on average 2 percentage points higher for women than for men, with an
interval from 0 to 4 points. Between 40 and 59 it is 17 points above
that of the youngest group.

Two things make these effects design-based. The average is taken with
the design weights, so it describes the population and not the sample.
The interval uses the variance of the design and the same t reference
with 9 degrees of freedom. The p-values of the two columns are close
without being equal (.019 and .011 for `Black`): a coefficient and its
average marginal effect are two different statistics.

## Testing a term: Wald and Rao-Scott

`race` enters the model with three coefficients, and one of them,
`Black`, has p = .019. That is not a test of race. With four groups,
one comparison in three below .05 is a weak basis, and the comparison
depends on the reference category. The question "does race belong in
this model" is a test of the three coefficients together.

`table_regression()` has no term-level test column for a design-based
fit. survey provides the tests:

```{r term-test}
regTermTest(fit, ~race)
regTermTest(fit, ~race, method = "LRT")
```

The first is a Wald test, F = 3.11 on 3 and 9 degrees of freedom,
p = .082. The second is the Rao-Scott test: the likelihood-ratio
statistic of the working model "where the observations are independent
and the weights are frequency weights", referred to a distribution that
accounts for the design (`?regTermTest`). It gives p = .274. The two
differ in size and agree on the reading: the data do not establish a
difference between the groups, whatever the single row says.

The result of such a test can be reported under the table with
`note_add`:

```{r term-test-note}
table_regression(
  fit,
  exponentiate = TRUE,
  show_columns = c("b", "ci", "p"),
  note_add = "Race: Wald F(3, 9) = 3.11, p = .082."
)
```

## Comparing models without a likelihood

Two models side by side, with and without race:

```{r compare}
fit0 <- svyglm(HI_CHOL ~ agecat + sex, design = dnh, family = quasibinomial)

table_regression(
  list("Age, sex" = fit0, "+ race" = fit),
  exponentiate = TRUE,
  show_columns = c("b", "ci", "p"),
  show_fit_stats = c("nobs", "aic", "eff_p")
)
```

The `AIC` row of a `svyglm()` fit is not the AIC of a `glm()`. survey
defines it "using the Rao-Scott approximation to the weighted
loglikelihood (Lumley and Scott, 2015). It replaces the usual penalty
term p [...] by the trace of the generalised design effect matrix"
(`?anova.svyglm`). `show_fit_stats = "eff_p"` displays that penalty as
`Effective parameters`. Here the model with race has seven coefficients
beyond the intercept and 12.9 effective parameters: under this design,
a coefficient costs more than one unit.

The criterion is lower without race, 5162.1 against 5166.0, which is
the reading of the two tests of the previous section. The design-based
AIC compares design-based fits of the same data. It should not be set
against the AIC of a `glm()` shown in another column.

survey also compares the two fits directly, with the same Rao-Scott
test as above:

```{r compare-anova}
anova(fit0, fit)
```

`nested = TRUE`, which adds the change statistics of a hierarchy to the
table, is refused for a design-based fit:

```{r nested-refused, error = TRUE}
table_regression(list(fit0, fit), nested = TRUE)
```

## Subpopulations

An analysis of a subgroup is a domain analysis, and the subgroup is
taken on the design, not on the data. "Estimates for subpopulations or
domains are handled by setting to zero the observed values for all
units that fall outside of the domain" (Binder, 2008, p. 192):
`subset()` on a design does this, "keeping the original design
information about number of clusters, strata" (`?subset.survey.design`).

```{r domain}
older <- subset(dnh, agecat == "(59,Inf]")
fit_old <- svyglm(HI_CHOL ~ race + sex, design = older, family = quasibinomial)
table_regression(fit_old, exponentiate = TRUE)
```

Among respondents of 60 and over, the odds ratio of women is 2.31, with
an interval from 1.56 to 3.42, against 1.24 in the whole sample. The
`n` row counts the 1,880 respondents of the domain, and the note counts
the PSUs that hold one of them, here all 31.

Subsetting the data first and declaring the design afterwards breaks
the design. For the smallest group, the design is declared without
complaint and the model stops:

```{r domain-wrong, error = TRUE}
other_data <- subset(nhanes, race == "Other")
d_other <- svydesign(
  id = ~SDMVPSU, strata = ~SDMVSTRA, weights = ~WTMEC2YR,
  nest = TRUE, data = other_data
)
svyglm(HI_CHOL ~ sex, design = d_other, family = quasibinomial)
```

One stratum has respondents of this group in a single PSU, and a
variance cannot be computed from one unit. That stratum has two PSUs in
the survey. Taken on the design, the same subgroup gives a model:

```{r domain-right}
fit_other <- svyglm(
  HI_CHOL ~ sex,
  design = subset(dnh, race == "Other"),
  family = quasibinomial
)
table_regression(fit_other, exponentiate = TRUE, show_columns = c("b", "ci", "p"))
```

The note counts 29 PSUs, those that hold a respondent of this group
with a cholesterol measure. In 15 strata they leave 14 degrees of
freedom for the design, and 13 for the tests of a model with one
predictor.

The error is not always that visible. For the high schools of the
cluster sample, present in 8 of the 15 districts, both routes give a
model, and their standard errors differ by 4%:

```{r domain-small}
high_design <- svyglm(api00 ~ ell + meals, design = subset(dclus1, stype == "H"))
high_data <- svyglm(
  api00 ~ ell + meals,
  design = svydesign(
    id = ~dnum, weights = ~pw, fpc = ~fpc,
    data = subset(apiclus1, stype == "H")
  )
)
table_regression(
  list("subset(design)" = high_design, "subset(data)" = high_data),
  show_columns = c("b", "se", "p")
)
```

The size of the error depends on the design, and nothing in the output
of the wrong route warns of it. Subsetting the design costs nothing and
is right in every case.

## Replicate weights

A design can be declared by replicate weights in place of strata and
clusters. "Some recent large-scale surveys specify replication weights
rather than the sampling design (partly for privacy reasons)"
(`?svrepdesign`). The functions are the same, and so are the
coefficients, which depend on the weights alone. The variance is
computed from the estimates obtained with each set of replicate
weights.

```{r replicate}
rclus1 <- as.svrepdesign(dclus1)
gl_rep <- svyglm(api00 ~ ell + meals + mobility, design = rclus1)

table_regression(
  list("Linearization" = gl, "Jackknife (JK1)" = gl_rep),
  show_columns = c("b", "se", "ci")
)
```

The note names the design of each model: the PSUs of the linearization,
the scheme and the number of replicates of the jackknife.
The jackknife and the linearization estimators "are approximately the
same for point estimates for which they are valid on large samples"
(Lee, 2008, p. 404). With 15 PSUs the sample of PSUs is not large, and
the two differ by 7% for the intercept and by 21% for `mobility`.

## Ordinal outcomes: `svyolr()`

`svyolr()` fits a cumulative logit model under the design. The API
score cut into three bands, on the stratified sample:

```{r ordinal}
apistrat$grade <- cut(
  apistrat$api00,
  c(0, 600, 700, 1000),
  labels = c("low", "mid", "high"),
  ordered_result = TRUE
)
dgrade <- svydesign(
  id = ~1, strata = ~stype, weights = ~pw, data = apistrat, fpc = ~fpc
)
ol <- svyolr(grade ~ ell + meals + stype, design = dgrade)
table_regression(ol, exponentiate = TRUE)
```

Under proportional odds one ratio applies to every cut of the scale:
each additional percentage point of pupils eligible for subsidized
meals multiplies the odds of a higher band by 0.90. The cut-points are
in a `Thresholds` block, on the log-odds scale and never exponentiated,
which the note states. There is no `AIC` row: survey has no such
criterion for a `svyolr()` fit.

The average marginal effects of an ordinal model come one column per
category of the outcome, and those of a predictor sum to zero across
the categories:

```{r ordinal-ame, eval = have_me}
table_regression(ol, show_columns = c("b", "ame"))
```

## Cox models: `svycoxph()`

The example of `?svycoxph`, which the help page itself introduces as a
"somewhat unrealistic example of nonresponse bias": the patients of the
Mayo Clinic data on primary biliary cholangitis who were randomized,
weighted by the inverse of an estimated probability of being
randomized.

```{r cox}
data(pbc, package = "survival")
pbc$randomized <- with(pbc, !is.na(trt) & trt > 0)
bias <- glm(randomized ~ age * edema, data = pbc, family = binomial)
pbc$randprob <- fitted(bias)

dpbc <- svydesign(
  id = ~1, prob = ~randprob, strata = ~edema,
  data = subset(pbc, randomized)
)
cx <- svycoxph(
  survival::Surv(time, status > 0) ~ log(bili) + protime + albumin,
  design = dpbc
)
table_regression(
  cx,
  exponentiate = TRUE,
  show_fit_stats = c("nobs", "weighted_nobs", "n_events", "concordance")
)
```

`prob` takes the probability, and survey inverts it: the weighted n is
the 418 patients of the cohort, for 312 in the analysis. The standard
errors are the design-based ones of survey, and the tests refer to a t
distribution with the residual degrees of freedom of the note. A list
of tokens in `show_fit_stats` replaces the default rows, so
`"weighted_nobs"` has to be named to stay in the table.

## What spicy refuses for survey fits, and why

A request that the design cannot honor gets an error that says why.

* `vcov =`. The variance of the design is the robust variance for the
  declared design. To change the estimator, change the design and
  refit. A `cluster =` is ignored with a warning that says the same.
* Statistics of a likelihood: `"bic"`, `"aicc"`, `"deviance"`,
  `"log_lik"` and the pseudo-R² tokens. The exception is `"aic"` for
  `svyglm()`, the design-based criterion of the previous sections.
* The AME columns of a `svycoxph()` model, as for any Cox model.
* `nested = TRUE` and the term-level test columns. The tests exist in
  survey, `regTermTest()` and `anova()`, and their result can be
  reported with `note_add`.
* `standardized`. Average marginal effects are the way to compare
  predictors on a common scale here.
* `ci_method = "profile"`, which needs a likelihood to profile.
* The RMST and risk-difference columns of a Cox model. Their
  uncertainty comes from resampling subjects, which ignores the strata
  and the clusters of the design. `survey::svykm()` gives a marginal
  survival curve under the design.
* `table_regression_uv()` on a design object. Fit each model with
  `svyglm()` and pass the fits to `table_regression()`.

```{r refusal, error = TRUE}
table_regression(fit, vcov = "HC3")
```

The refusal of the RMST and risk-difference columns rests on a
measurement. On simulated data, over five designs and three seeds, a
bootstrap of the rows gave a contrast between clusters a standard error
too small by a factor of 1.5 to 6, depending on the number and the size
of the clusters (about 3 for 30 clusters of 25 units with a moderate
intra-cluster correlation). A contrast within clusters came out about
right, and so did a design without intra-cluster correlation. The
ratios are the same for the Cox coefficients themselves: this is the
ordinary design effect, carried onto the RMST and the risk difference.

## Presentation-ready output

Everything above renders through the rich output engines. The
comparison of the two NHANES models as a `gt` table:

```{r rich, eval = build_rich_tables && have_gt}
pkgdown_dark_gt(
  table_regression(
    list("Age, sex" = fit0, "+ race" = fit),
    exponentiate = TRUE,
    show_columns = c("b", "ci", "p"),
    output = "gt"
  )
)
```
